title: Teaching in the Age of School Choice
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: In this condensed keynote, Pondiscio argues that universal school choice and education savings accounts are ending the district monopoly on schooling, and that the teaching profession must adapt to a pluralistic, entrepreneurial market of charters, microschools, co-ops and virtual platforms. He recounts his own South Bronx classroom and the pandemic pods that foreshadowed this shift, and he faults ed schools for poorly preparing teachers. He then turns critic from within the choice camp, naming three risks: unequal access that favours the affluent, limited teacher capacity because the nation needs nearly four million ordinary teachers, and loss of shared civic culture. His proposed answer is to pair choice with quality: better teacher training, equitable access, and a shared core curriculum. Because the piece is about where and how teachers will work, it fits Practice & Culture, the closest home for his profession and policy commentary.
points: Choice is changing who can provide education as well as who receives it, so teachers will need entrepreneurial, adaptable skills for charters, microschools, co-ops and virtual settings.
Pondiscio holds that ed schools have failed teachers, with his air traffic controller analogy showing how little practical preparation they give.
Reforms must be doable by the ordinary teachers the system actually has, since nearly four million are needed, not by heroic ones.
A choice-driven system risks a two-tier outcome, with non-choosers left in schools of last resort and shared civic culture fraying.
His remedy is a common core curriculum across diverse schools, giving pluralism with coherence.
quotes: It’s no longer taken for granted that your local public school is the only game in town. Parents are asking: “Is this school the best I can do for my child? If not, what else is out there—and how do I get it?

Universal school choice, empowered by education savings accounts (ESAs), is decentralizing education, giving families unprecedented control over where and how their children learn. Once Texas adopts and implements ESAs, half of America’s families will have the power to opt out of traditional public schools and take the money with them.

For years I’ve joked darkly that if we trained air traffic controllers the way we trained teachers, students would write papers about structural inequities in transportation and work on developing their personal philosophy of air travel. “Landing planes? Oh, that’s something you learn on the job. We’re not here to train you.

This risks a two-tier system: affluent families in high-quality schools and settings; “non-choosers”—typically the most disadvantaged—left behind in struggling public schools that may become something like schools of last resort.

If achievable, sustainable progress is our aim—and it must be our aim—the job has to be doable by the teachers we have, not the teachers we wish we had. Let’s be honest: Almost anyone can teach students who are motivated, curious, and engaged.

E.D. Hirsch, Jr., warned us that schools are “the central and main hope for the preservation of democratic ideals.” In a choice-driven system, how do we ensure students in, for example, an Austin microschool, a Houston magnet, or a Dallas Catholic school share some common knowledge and civic preparation? One solution is curriculum.

But to sustain it, we must pair choice with quality: training teachers to be successful in news settings and in new models, ensuring equitable access, and taking curriculum seriously to drive academic and civic outcomes. We’re at a crossroads.
